summary: An array is a fixed-size block of same-typed elements stored contiguously in memory and accessed by zero-based index. Because the layout is contiguous, indexing is O(1), and arrays are the foundation under strings, matrices, buffers, and most data structures.

sections.heading: Declaring and initializing
sections.body: The size is fixed at declaration (a constant expression, or a runtime value for a C99 variable-length array). Elements not covered by an initializer list are zero-filled; arrays with static storage duration are zero-initialized by default, while automatic arrays hold garbage.
sections.code:
int a[5];                    // uninitialized (automatic)
int b[5] = {2, 4, 8};        // 2 4 8 0 0
int c[] = {1, 2, 3};         // size deduced: 3
int d[6] = {[2] = 7, [5] = 9};  // designated (C99): 0 0 7 0 0 9
static int e[100];           // all zero

sections.heading: Indexing and bounds
sections.body: Valid indices run from 0 to n-1. C never checks bounds: a[n] or a[-1] is undefined behavior and can silently corrupt neighbouring variables or crash. Looping with the wrong bound is the classic off-by-one bug.
sections.code: for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) b[i] *= 2;   // < 5, never <= 5

sections.heading: Size of an array
sections.body: `sizeof` on a real array yields its total byte size, so the element count is `sizeof a / sizeof a[0]`. This only works where the array itself is in scope; once passed to a function it has decayed to a pointer and sizeof gives the pointer's size.
sections.code: int n = sizeof b / sizeof b[0];   // 5

sections.heading: Arrays and functions
sections.body: Arrays are passed by address: the name decays to a pointer to the first element, so the callee can modify the caller's elements but does not know the length. Always pass the length as a separate parameter.
sections.code:
void fill(int *a, size_t n, int v) { for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = v; }
fill(b, 5, 0);

sections.heading: Multidimensional arrays
sections.body: A 2D array is an array of arrays laid out in row-major order: all of row 0, then row 1, and so on. When passing it, every dimension except the first must be given so the compiler can compute row strides.

subtopics.title: Array decay
subtopics.summary: When an array becomes a pointer.

sections.body: In most expressions an array name is converted to a pointer to its first element. Exceptions: operand of sizeof, operand of &, and a string literal initializing a char array. That is why `&a` has type `int (*)[5]` while `a` decays to `int *`.
sections.code:
int a[5];
int *p = a;          // &a[0]
int (*pa)[5] = &a;   // pointer to the whole array
printf("%zu %zu\n", sizeof a, sizeof p);  // 20 8

sections.body: `int v[n];` allocates n elements on the stack at run time. It is convenient but a large or attacker-controlled n overflows the stack, and VLAs became optional in C11. Prefer malloc for sizes you do not control.

subtopics.title: Arrays versus pointers
subtopics.summary: They are not the same thing.

bullets: An array owns storage; a pointer holds an address.
sizeof differs: whole array versus pointer size.
An array name is not assignable; a pointer is.
They convert freely in expressions, which hides the difference.
Linear scan for sum, min, max.
Two pointers from both ends (reverse, palindrome).
Prefix sums for fast range queries.

sections.body: Strengths: O(1) random access, cache-friendly contiguous layout, no per-element overhead. Limits: fixed size, O(n) insertion and deletion in the middle, no bounds checking. For growth, use a heap block you realloc (a dynamic array).

takeaways: No bounds checking: out-of-range access is undefined behavior.
Arrays decay to pointers when passed; pass the length separately.
2D arrays are row-major; callee needs all but the first dimension.
